name: Sodium Oxybate (Xyrem, Lumryz)
summary: Powerful nighttime CNS depressant for narcolepsy with cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness. Very fast onset, high sodium load, boxed warnings for respiratory depression, abuse, and REMS-only access.
description: Sodium oxybate (brand names Xyrem and Lumryz) is a potent central nervous system depressant used at night to treat narcolepsy with cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness. It is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a substance that exists naturally in the brain but is also used illicitly as a "club drug." At therapeutic doses, sodium oxybate can deepen nighttime sleep and improve daytime alertness and cataplexy. At the same time, it carries serious risks: respiratory depression, sudden loss of consciousness, complex sleep behaviors, mood changes, and a high potential for abuse and misuse. It also delivers a substantial sodium load, which can aggravate heart, kidney, or blood pressure problems. Because of these dangers, sodium oxybate is available only through strict REMS programs and must be taken exactly as directed.
patient_summary: Sodium oxybate (Xyrem, Lumryz) is a strong nighttime medicine for narcolepsy. It can help you sleep more deeply at night so your daytime sleepiness and cataplexy improve. But it is also powerful and risky. The active ingredient is related to GHB, a drug that can be abused. Even at prescribed doses, sodium oxybate can slow your breathing, knock you out quickly, and cause strange sleep behaviors like sleepwalking or doing things you don’t remember. It also contains a lot of sodium (salt), which can be a problem if you have heart, kidney, or blood pressure issues. Because of these risks, it is tightly controlled through special REMS programs, and doses must be carefully measured, mixed, and taken on an empty stomach while you are already in bed.

metadata.controlled_substance: Schedule III (US medical use); Schedule I for illicit GHB

linked_conditions.context: Approved for the treatment of cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness in adults and in pediatric patients 7 years and older with narcolepsy.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to sodium oxybate or any component of the formulation (Canadian labeling)

efficacy_response.metric: Improvement in daytime sleepiness and cataplexy
efficacy_response.patient_text: In clinical use, many patients have fewer cataplexy attacks and less overwhelming daytime sleepiness once they reach a stable sodium oxybate dose, but not everyone can tolerate the side effects, and careful titration is required.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid; significant first-pass metabolism; high-fat meals delay and blunt peak levels.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Short-acting; requires 2 nightly doses for sustained effect
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Once-nightly ER dose intended to cover the night
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily via the Krebs cycle to carbon dioxide and water; secondarily via beta-oxidation; no active metabolites; saturable metabolism
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily as carbon dioxide via the lungs; <5% excreted unchanged in urine; negligible fecal excretion
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat meals delay absorption (Tmax ↑ ~1–1.25 hours) and reduce Cmax by ~33–59% and AUC by ~14–37%. Take at least 2 hours after eating.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Sodium oxybate is a targeted treatment for narcolepsy-related symptoms, not a general sleep aid.
items: {link:condition:narcolepsy:Narcolepsy with Cataplexy}: Reduces the number and severity of sudden loss-of-muscle-tone episodes triggered by emotions (cataplexy).
{link:condition:narcolepsy:Narcolepsy with Excessive Daytime Sleepiness}: Deepens night sleep to improve daytime wakefulness and functioning in people with narcolepsy.
Nighttime sleep consolidation: Helps stabilize fragmented sleep so the brain gets more restorative slow-wave sleep.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Experiences on sodium oxybate vary widely, but these patterns show up often in clinical practice:

quotes: Once I take it, I’m out in 5 to 10 minutes.
There’s a narrow window after drinking it—then I’m suddenly very sleepy.
If I’m not already in bed, I feel unsafe because I get drowsy so fast.
items.note: Onset is rapid (usually within 5–15 minutes). Patients must be in bed before dosing.

quotes: My sleep feels deeper, less broken up.
My cataplexy attacks got less frequent once we found the right dose.
Daytime sleepiness is still there, but it’s not crushing like before.
If I get up at night, I’m wobbly and off-balance.
Sometimes I wake up feeling like I have a drug hangover.
I’ve learned not to walk around after I take it unless absolutely necessary.
items.note: Dizziness, drowsiness, and impaired coordination are common and can increase fall risk.

quotes: My dreams are vivid and sometimes bizarre.
My partner says I talk or move around in my sleep.
There were nights when I apparently got up, but I barely remember it.
items.note: Parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep talking, sleep eating, night terrors, sleep driving) and amnestic episodes have been reported.

quotes: My mood felt flatter and more irritable after starting it.
I noticed dark thoughts creeping in that I hadn’t had for a while.
We had to closely watch my depression and adjust other meds.
items.note: Depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts have been reported; anyone with a past history needs extra monitoring.

quotes: I lost some weight without really trying.
Nighttime bedwetting was embarrassing but part of the package.
I feel puffy if I don’t watch my salt, because this medicine has a lot of sodium.
items.note: Weight loss, urinary incontinence, and sodium-related fluid shifts can occur, especially in children and adolescents.

sections.heading: US Boxed Warnings & Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Strong CNS depressant with risk of respiratory depression, loss of consciousness, abuse, and misuse. Access is restricted through REMS programs.
sections.black_box: Sodium oxybate is a central nervous system (CNS) depressant. At recommended doses, obtundation and clinically significant respiratory depression have occurred in clinical trials. Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB). Abuse or misuse of illicit GHB, especially when combined with other CNS depressants, has been associated with seizures, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness, coma, and death. Because of these risks, sodium oxybate is only available through restricted REMS programs (Lumryz REMS or Xywav and Xyrem REMS).
other: CNS depression: Impairs mental alertness and motor coordination. Patients must avoid hazardous activities (like driving) for at least 6 hours after a dose.
Respiratory depression: Can slow or suppress breathing, especially in people with underlying respiratory disease or when combined with other CNS depressants.
Behavioral and psychiatric effects: Associated with aggression, agitation, anxiety, confusion, emotional lability, depression, paranoia, psychosis, hallucinations, panic attacks, and suicidality.
Parasomnias: Sleepwalking and complex sleep behaviors (including sleep driving and sleep eating) have been reported.
High sodium load: Each nightly dose delivers substantial sodium; may worsen heart failure, hypertension, or kidney disease.
Abuse, misuse, diversion: Because sodium oxybate is closely related to illicit GHB, it has significant abuse potential. Misuse has been associated with blackouts, amnesia, and serious toxicity.
Withdrawal/tolerance: Tolerance and withdrawal have been reported at higher illicit doses, though not clearly defined at therapeutic doses.
patient_counseling: Never combine sodium oxybate with alcohol or sleeping pills. This can stop your breathing and be fatal.
Only take doses on an empty stomach—at least 2 hours after eating—and while you are already in bed.
Expect to fall asleep within 5–15 minutes; you may not feel drowsy first, it can be sudden.
For 2-dose regimens, set an alarm for the second dose. If you sleep through it, skip it—do not double up.
Tell your prescriber immediately about new or worsening depression, anxiety, irritability, or any suicidal thoughts.
Ask a bed partner to watch for sleepwalking, strange nighttime behaviors, or breathing pauses and to report them.
Because this medicine contains a lot of sodium, talk with your clinician about heart, kidney, or blood pressure issues and your overall salt intake.
Store the medication and mixed doses securely away from children and others; never share it with anyone.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common effects include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, headache, weight loss, and urinary incontinence. Serious risks include respiratory depression, severe mood and behavior changes, parasomnias, and abuse-related harms.
plain_language_list: Nighttime bedwetting or needing to urinate at night
Sleepwalking or doing things in your sleep you don’t remember

common.patient_note: Weight loss may be noticeable in children and adolescents. Regular weight checks are important, especially if appetite is poor or vomiting is frequent.

Nausea and vomiting are common during titration. Taking doses exactly as directed (on an empty stomach with proper dilution) can help. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep doses down requires medical attention.
Nighttime bedwetting can be distressing but is a known side effect. Practical strategies (protective bedding, bathroom planning) and possible dose adjustments can help.
Some people feel confused, disoriented, or "out of it," especially at night or shortly after dosing. This is a safety concern around stairs, bathrooms, and other hazards.
You may feel dizzy, very sleepy, or as if you are intoxicated. Avoid getting out of bed unless absolutely necessary and move slowly if you must stand.
Headaches can occur, sometimes more often in older adults. Persistent or severe headaches should prompt reassessment.
New or worsening anxiety, low mood, irritability, or emotional swings should be monitored closely. Suicidal thoughts are an emergency.
You may notice increased sweating or feeling clammy, especially at night. This can be uncomfortable but is usually not dangerous by itself.
Sleepwalking and complex sleep behaviors may put you at risk for injury. Bed partners often notice this first. Any concerning behaviors should be reported immediately.
Some patients report limb or joint discomfort. This is rarely dangerous but can affect quality of life.

serious: Respiratory depression and oxygen desaturation, including sleep apnea and central sleep apnea.
Severe CNS depression, obtundation, and delirium with impaired consciousness.
Serious psychiatric reactions: aggression, agitation, paranoia, psychosis (including acute psychosis), hallucinations, emotional lability, and panic attacks.
Suicidal ideation and suicidal tendencies in adults and pediatric patients.
Complex parasomnias, including sleep driving and sleep eating, with risk of injury.
Cardiovascular effects: hypertension and fluid retention (postmarketing).
Severe falls or injuries related to sedation, dizziness, or parasomnias.
Abuse-related harms: overdose, blackouts, and life-threatening toxicity when misused or combined with other depressants.

sections.heading: Drug, Sodium, & Food Interactions
sections.intro: Sodium oxybate is highly interactive with other CNS depressants and delivers a large sodium load. Food strongly affects how quickly and how much drug is absorbed.

items.risk: Profound CNS depression, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
items.action: Absolute contraindication. Do not use sodium oxybate if you drink alcohol; do not drink alcohol at any point while on therapy.

items.risk: Markedly increased risk of respiratory depression, severe sedation, hypotension, and loss of consciousness.
items.action: Contraindicated. Avoid all sedative-hypnotic agents with sodium oxybate.

items.with: Other CNS Depressants (opioids, sedating antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiseizure agents, muscle relaxants, general anesthetics, illicit depressants)
items.risk: Additive or synergistic CNS and respiratory depression, hypotension, and risk of death.
items.action: Avoid whenever possible. If no alternative exists, use the lowest effective doses with very close monitoring by experienced clinicians.

items.risk: Worsening hypertension, heart failure, or kidney disease due to cumulative sodium burden.
items.action: Monitor total daily sodium intake. Counsel patients with cardiovascular or renal disease to restrict dietary sodium and consider alternative treatments if the sodium load is unsafe.

items.risk: Delayed absorption and reduced peak levels, which may blunt effect and alter timing of sleep onset.
items.action: Administer sodium oxybate at least 2 hours after eating; avoid high-fat meals close to dosing.

items.risk: Dose stacking, overdose, and severe CNS depression.
items.action: Do not combine oxybate formulations. When switching between IR Xyrem and ER Lumryz, use the nearest equivalent total nightly dose as directed.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Sodium oxybate is designed to act quickly at night to deepen sleep, with immediate-release and extended-release options.
key_points: Onset: Rapid—most people fall asleep within 5–15 minutes after each dose.
Peak Levels: Immediate-release Xyrem peaks in about 30–75 minutes; extended-release Lumryz peaks around 90 minutes.
Half-life: About 30–60 minutes, with saturable metabolism.
Duration: IR requires 2 nightly doses (bedtime and 2.5–4 hours later); ER Lumryz is taken once nightly and is intended to cover the night.
Food: Taking it right after a high-fat meal delays onset and reduces peak levels, which can disrupt timing.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Sodium oxybate dosing is highly individualized. Doses are titrated slowly based on response and side effects, and differ by formulation (Xyrem IR vs Lumryz ER), age, and weight.

narcolepsy.immediate_release_xyrem: Start with 2.25 g at bedtime after the patient is in bed, followed by 2.25 g 2.5–4 hours later (total 4.5 g per night). Increase total nightly dose by 1.5 g per week (0.75 g added to each dose) as tolerated and needed. Usual effective range: 6–9 g per night; maximum: 9 g per night.
narcolepsy.extended_release_lumryz: Start with 4.5 g once nightly at bedtime. May increase by 1.5 g per night at weekly intervals based on efficacy and tolerability. Recommended range: 6–9 g once nightly; maximum: 9 g per night.

adult.missed_second_dose: If the second IR dose is missed, skip it and resume the regular two-dose schedule the next night. Do not take two doses at once.
adult.switching_ir_to_er: When switching from Xyrem IR to Lumryz ER, use the nearest total equivalent dose (g/night) as a single bedtime dose, as guided by the prescriber.
adult.elderly: Use the same dosing principles as adults but start low and titrate slowly. Older adults are more vulnerable to headache, confusion, falls, and respiratory effects.

hepatic.immediate_release_xyrem: Reduce the initial IR dose by 50% and titrate cautiously, as exposure (AUC) is doubled and clearance is reduced in cirrhosis.
hepatic.extended_release_lumryz: Do not use Lumryz as initial therapy in hepatic impairment; only consider switching to ER after a stable maintenance dose is established on IR and an appropriate ER strength is available.

adult.renal: No specific adjustment is provided, but use caution due to high sodium content and potential fluid overload in kidney disease.

sections.simple_explanation: Most adults start with a lower nightly dose and increase slowly each week until daytime symptoms improve and side effects are tolerable. Immediate-release Xyrem uses two doses per night; extended-release Lumryz uses a single bedtime dose.

pediatric_narcolepsy_ir_xyrem.under_20kg: Initial total nightly dose 60–90 mg/kg/night divided into 2 doses (bedtime and 2.5–4 hours later). Titrate every 1–2 weeks based on response. Reported maximum total dose: 180 mg/kg/night.
pediatric_narcolepsy_ir_xyrem.20_to_less_than_30kg: Initial ≤1 g at bedtime and ≤1 g 2.5–4 hours later. After 1 week, increase by ≤0.5 g per dose (1 g per night) each week based on efficacy and tolerability. Maximum single dose: 3 g; maximum nightly dose: 6 g.
pediatric_narcolepsy_ir_xyrem.30_to_less_than_45kg: Initial ≤1.5 g at bedtime and ≤1.5 g 2.5–4 hours later. After 1 week, increase by ≤0.5 g per dose (1 g per night) each week. Maximum single dose: 3.75 g; maximum nightly dose: 7.5 g.
pediatric_narcolepsy_ir_xyrem.45kg_and_above: Initial ≤2.25 g at bedtime and ≤2.25 g 2.5–4 hours later. After 1 week, increase by ≤0.75 g per dose (1.5 g per night) each week. Maximum single dose: 4.5 g; maximum nightly dose: 9 g.

pediatric_narcolepsy_er_lumryz.20_to_less_than_45kg: ER Lumryz is not suitable for initial therapy at these weights because appropriate packet strengths to allow reduced starting doses are not available. Start with IR Xyrem; once a stable effective total nightly dose is reached, convert to the nearest ER dose. Maximum nightly doses remain: 6 g for 20–<30 kg and 7.5 g for 30–<45 kg.
pediatric_narcolepsy_er_lumryz.45kg_and_above: Initial ER dose 4.5 g once nightly at bedtime; may titrate by 1.5 g per week based on efficacy and tolerability, up to 9 g per night.

pediatric_hepatic_impairment.immediate_release_xyrem: Reduce total nightly dose by 50% and give in 2 divided doses.
pediatric_hepatic_impairment.extended_release_lumryz: Do not use ER Lumryz to initiate therapy in children with any degree of liver impairment; only consider switching once a stable IR dose is established and an appropriate ER strength exists.

sections.heading: Available Formulations & Sodium Content
sections.text: Sodium oxybate is available as an immediate-release oral solution and an extended-release powder packet for oral suspension. Both formulations contain significant sodium.
items: Immediate-Release Oral Solution (US & Canada): Xyrem and generics 500 mg/mL (180 mL bottles).
Extended-Release Oral Suspension Packets (US): Lumryz 4.5 g, 6 g, 7.5 g, and 9 g single-dose packets; also supplied as starter packs with multiple strengths.
Sodium content by total nightly dose: 3 g ≈ 550 mg sodium; 4.5 g ≈ 820 mg; 6 g ≈ 1,100 mg; 7.5 g ≈ 1,400 mg; 9 g ≈ 1,640 mg.
High sodium load: Clinically important for patients with heart failure, hypertension, kidney disease, or those on sodium-restricted diets.

sections.heading: How to Take It
sections.text: Sodium oxybate requires precise preparation, timing, and safety precautions for both IR and ER formulations.
key_points: Take on an empty stomach: at least 2 hours after eating.
Always administer while the patient is in bed (or sitting up in bed), then lie down immediately and stay in bed.
Immediate-release (Xyrem):
- Two nightly doses: first at bedtime, second 2.5–4 hours later.
- Prepare both doses before bed, diluting each with ~60 mL (~1/4 cup) water in the provided containers and securing child-resistant caps.
- Use diluted doses within 24 hours; rinse containers in the morning.
Extended-release (Lumryz):
- Single bedtime dose. Fill mixing cup to line A with ~80 mL (~1/3 cup) cool/cold water, pour in packet contents, close lid, and shake for at least 60 seconds. Do not use hot water.
- Drink within 30 minutes. Then fill the cup to line B with water, shake 10 seconds, and drink to capture any remaining medication.
Pediatric administration:
- Give doses while the child is sitting up in bed, then have them lie down immediately.
- Sleep typically occurs within 5–15 minutes and may feel abrupt.
Missed second dose (IR):
- If the second dose is missed, skip it and resume the next night.
- Never take two doses at the same time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Use of sodium oxybate in special populations requires careful risk–benefit analysis, with special attention to sodium load and respiratory, cardiovascular, and psychiatric risks.
sections.pregnancy: Sodium oxybate crosses the placenta. When used as an anesthetic during labor, it has been associated with slightly lower Apgar scores due to neonatal sleepiness. Data on therapeutic use in pregnancy are limited. Use only if potential benefits clearly outweigh risks and alternative treatments are not suitable.
sections.lactation: GHB is naturally present in breast milk and increases with sodium oxybate therapy. Limited data suggest avoiding breastfeeding between the two bedtime doses and for 6–8 hours after the second dose to reduce infant exposure. The decision to continue breastfeeding should weigh the benefits of breastfeeding, the importance of therapy to the mother, and potential risks to the infant.
sections.pediatrics: Approved for narcolepsy with cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness in patients ≥7 years. Pediatric dosing is weight-based and typically uses the IR formulation for initiation. Children and adolescents may be more prone to weight loss, urinary incontinence, and behavioral effects and require close monitoring.
sections.geriatrics: Limited data suggest a higher incidence of headaches and potentially increased vulnerability to CNS effects in older adults (≥65 years). Use extra caution, start low, titrate slowly, and monitor for cognitive changes, falls, and respiratory issues.
sections.hepatic: In cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A and C), AUC is doubled, half-life is prolonged, and clearance is reduced. IR dosing should begin at 50% of the usual starting dose with slow titration. ER Lumryz should not be used to start therapy in patients with hepatic impairment.
sections.renal: Although only a small amount of drug is excreted unchanged in urine, the high sodium content can worsen renal and cardiovascular conditions. Use with caution in patients with kidney disease and those on sodium-restricted diets.
sections.cardiovascular: Because of high sodium content and risk of fluid retention, use cautiously in heart failure, hypertension, and other cardiovascular disease. Monitor blood pressure, volume status, and overall sodium load.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and suicidality: new or worsening depression, suicidal ideation, suicidal behavior.
Behavioral and psychiatric symptoms: aggression, agitation, emotional lability, anxiety, confusion, paranoia, psychosis, hallucinations, panic attacks.
CNS depression and motor function: level of alertness, coordination, falls, ability to avoid hazardous activities for at least 6 hours after dosing.

Respiratory status: signs of respiratory depression, central or obstructive sleep apnea, and oxygen desaturation (especially in patients with obesity, narcolepsy, or pre-existing breathing disorders).
Sleep-related behaviors: sleepwalking, sleep driving, sleep eating, and other parasomnias; evaluate for injury risk and safety concerns.
Weight and nutrition: weight loss and appetite, particularly in children and adolescents.
Genitourinary effects: urinary incontinence and nocturia.
Sodium-related effects: blood pressure, edema, heart failure symptoms, and kidney function in patients at risk.
Signs of abuse, misuse, and diversion: early refill requests, dose escalation, multiple prescribers or pharmacies, inconsistent histories, or evidence of recreational use.
Adherence to REMS requirements and safe storage/disposal instructions.

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a metabolite of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). Its therapeutic effects are thought to be mediated mainly through GABAB receptor activity on noradrenergic, dopaminergic, and thalamocortical neurons. In practical terms, it applies a strong "brake" to certain arousal circuits at night, promoting deep slow-wave sleep and stabilizing the sleep–wake system. This can reduce daytime sleepiness and cataplexy in narcolepsy, although the exact mechanisms are still being studied.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment
sections.text: Sodium oxybate is a specialized therapy reserved for moderate to severe narcolepsy with cataplexy or marked daytime sleepiness when other approaches are not enough. It is usually prescribed and monitored by clinicians with experience in sleep medicine and psychopharmacology. Because of its boxed warnings, REMS restrictions, abuse potential, complex dosing, and high sodium content, sodium oxybate is not appropriate for routine insomnia or milder sleep complaints. Mixed-salt oxybate (Xywav) may be favored when sodium load is a major concern, whereas sodium oxybate may be used where its particular formulation or accessibility is preferred and the sodium burden is acceptable.

faqs.q: What is sodium oxybate used for?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate (Xyrem, Lumryz) is used at night to treat narcolepsy in adults and in children 7 years and older. It helps with cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone) and excessive daytime sleepiness by deepening nighttime sleep and stabilizing the sleep–wake cycle.

faqs.q: How is sodium oxybate different from Xywav?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate and Xywav share the same active moiety (GHB) and similar clinical effects, but Xywav is a mixed-salt oxybate with much less sodium. Sodium oxybate carries a higher sodium load, which can matter for people with high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney problems. Both products are only available through REMS programs and carry similar boxed warnings for CNS depression and abuse.

faqs.q: How fast does sodium oxybate work?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate works quickly—most people fall asleep within 5 to 15 minutes of taking a dose. Because the onset is so rapid, doses must be taken in bed (or sitting up in bed), followed by lying down immediately.

faqs.q: Why does sodium oxybate have a boxed warning?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate is a strong CNS depressant and the sodium salt of GHB, a drug of abuse. It can cause respiratory depression and marked decreases in consciousness, even at prescribed doses. Illicit GHB misuse has been linked to seizures, coma, and death, particularly when combined with other sedatives or alcohol. These risks led to boxed warnings and REMS-only access.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking sodium oxybate?
faqs.a: No. You must not drink alcohol while taking sodium oxybate. The combination can cause severe sedation, dangerously slow breathing, coma, and death. Alcohol use with this medication is an absolute contraindication.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Xyrem and Lumryz?
faqs.a: Xyrem is an immediate-release oral solution that is taken twice each night (one dose at bedtime and another 2.5–4 hours later). Lumryz is an extended-release powder packet that you mix with water and take once nightly at bedtime. Both contain sodium oxybate and require REMS enrollment, but their dosing schedules and preparation steps differ.

faqs.q: What if I miss my second Xyrem dose?
faqs.a: If you miss the second nightly dose of Xyrem, skip it. Do not take two doses at once or make up the missed dose. Resume your usual two-dose schedule the next night.

faqs.q: Why is the sodium content important?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate contains a large amount of sodium. At a 9 g nightly dose, you receive about 1,640 mg of sodium just from the medication. This added sodium can worsen high blood pressure, heart failure, and kidney disease. Your clinician will consider your overall sodium intake and health conditions when deciding if this medication is appropriate.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of sodium oxybate?
faqs.a: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, headaches, sweating, weight loss (especially in children and teens), urinary incontinence, and feeling intoxicated or very drowsy. Sleepwalking and other unusual sleep behaviors can also occur. Many side effects improve with time or dose adjustments, but any severe or persistent symptoms should be discussed with your prescriber.

faqs.q: Can sodium oxybate affect my mood or cause suicidal thoughts?
faqs.a: Yes. Sodium oxybate has been associated with depression, anxiety, emotional swings, and suicidal thoughts or behaviors. People with a history of depression or suicide attempts may be at higher risk. Any new or worsening mood symptoms, hopelessness, or thoughts of self-harm are emergencies and require immediate evaluation.

faqs.q: Is sodium oxybate safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Sodium oxybate crosses the placenta and appears in breast milk. Data are limited, but fetal and infant exposure can lead to sedation and breathing problems. Decisions about using it during pregnancy or breastfeeding must be individualized and made with a clinician who understands your sleep disorder and overall medical situation.
